Vasantapañcamī
------------------------------------------
वसन्तपञ्चमी (Māgha-śukla-pañcamī, the 5th day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, usually in February) is a day dedicated to the worship of सरस्वती, the goddess of learning and fine-arts. The worship is done to clay image and then immersed in a river or a tank. It is an extremely popular festival in Bengal, especially among students.
Vasantapañcamī is also called श्रीपञ्चमी, Śrī being सरस्वती.

vāsanā
(‘[a strong impression] that lives in the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
The word वासना is generally interpreted as saṁskāra, a strong impression in the मिन्द्, carried over from previous lives. It is so strong that, when it arises in the मिन्द्, a person is forced to act without thinking of the consequences.
It is classified into two kinds, malinā (impure) and śuddhā (pure). The former leads to the bondage of transmigration whereas the latter helps in getting लिबेरतिओन्.
The malinavāsanā, again, is of three kinds: lokavāsanā (desire to please others); śāstravāsanā (desire for dry intellectual knowledge); dehavāsanā (desire to keep the body healthy and beautiful).
All these three vāsanās have to be eschewed.
As for the śuddhavāsanās, there is no particular way of classification. Some of the disciplines or qualities listed under these, which help to eradicate the evil vāsanās are: मैत्री (friendship), karuṇā (compassion), mudita (feeling happy in the happiness of others) and upekṣā (indifference towards the sinners) (vide Yogasūtras 1.33).
The twenty-six qualities like abhaya (fearlessness), दम (self-control), स्वाध्याय (study of the holy scriptures), तपस् (austerities), अहिṁसा (non-violence) and ārjava (straightforwardness) described in the Bhagavadgītā (1

) also help in creating śuddhavāsanās.
The natural qualities of greatness of a perfect being described in the second, twelfth and fourteenth chapters of the Bhagavadgītā, if practised as modes of sādhana, will lead to the production of pure vāsanās that ultimately lead to लिबेरतिओन्.

Vāsuki
------------------------------------------
Vāsuki is one of the eight well-known serpents of paurāṇic celebrity. Nāgarāja and Nāgendra are his other names.
He was an offspring of कश्यप and कद्रू. He is described as one of the seven dragons holding the earth on his hoods.
He was used as a rope wound round the mountain मन्दर at the time of churning the milky ocean.
Śataśīrṣā was his wife and जरत्कारु was his sister.
Vāsuki is also, sometimes, described as one of the dikpālas (guardians of directions) presiding over the downward direction.

Vasiṣṭha
------------------------------------------
Vasiṣṭha is one of the most well-known sages, mentioned several times even in the Ṛgveda (vide 7.33.14).
VasiṣṭhaAccording to one version he was one of the mānasaputras or मिन्द्-born sons of the creator ब्रह्मा. According to another version, he was born in a kumbha (or pot) as the son of the deity वरुण. अगस्त्य, another great sage, was his twin.
Arundhatī—also known as अक्षमाला and Ūrjā—was his wife. The sage शक्ति was his son. Sages पराशर and व्यास were his grandson and great-grandson respectively.
He was the rājaguru—royal preceptor—to the kings of the इक्ष्वाकु race.
There are several legends eulogising his greatness.
The king Viśvaratha, son of Gādhi, tried his best to take away by force the divine cow Nandinī from वसिष्ठ but failed miserably. After several rounds of तपस्, he too became a ब्रह्मर्षि (a sage of the highest order), later on known as विश्वामित्र.
Vasiṣṭha was one among the सप्तर्षिस् (the seven divine sages) and also a gotrapravartaka (person who started a गोत्र or lineage).

Vasantarāja-śakuna
(‘Vasantarāja’s [treatise on] prognosticatory signs’)
------------------------------------------
People of all countries and civilisations have believed in prognosticatory signs from times immemorial. Such beliefs persist even now.
The Sanskrit word for such a pro-gnostication is शकुन (See ŚAKUNA for details.)
Though the literature on the śakunas is quite extensive, mostly spread over the पुराणस्, there are also works which deal with this subject in a specialised way. Out of these, the Vasantarājaśakuna of Vasantarāja (circa A.

) is an independent and exhaustive work on this subject. It contains 1520 verses in 20 vargas or chapters. It has a commentary by Bhānucandragaṇi (16th century A. D.).
Vasantarāja was the son of विजय-rājabhaṭṭa and सरस्वती. He was honoured by the king Candradeva of मिथिला and wrote this work at his request. He mentions several works of an earlier period and pays his respects to many of the ancient sages like अत्रि, वसिष्ठ and व्यास who had declared the knowledge of the śakunas.
The following is a brief account of the subjects dealt with: authenticity of the śakunaśāstra; honouring the गुरु and the eight लोकपालस् like इन्द्र; on directions and distances of factors associated with śakunas; signs of auspiciousness or otherwise, as applied to men and women; on birds and their chirpings; signs as applied to animals; barking of dogs and howling of jackals; importance of this śāstra or science.
A notable feature of this work is that 781 verses—more than half—have been devoted to the sounds of birds.

Vāsudevopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmaveda group.
It is a short work in the form of a dialogue between the sage नारद and Lord वासुदेव, mostly in the anuṣṭubh metre interspersed with prose sentences.
The main theme is how to prepare and wear the त्रिपुण्ड्र mark with the yellow clay called गोपीचन्दन, on different parts of the body.
Parts of the body on which the त्रिपुण्ड्र has to be inscribed are: forehead, neck, arms and the chest. A saṁnyāsin, in addition, has to wear it on the top of the shaven head also.
Various Vedic mantras as also the प्रणव (Oṅkāra) are to be used while marking.

Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtras
------------------------------------------
Belonging to the period 300-100 B. C., the Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtras is a fairly ancient work. Though assigned to the Kalpasūtra group of the Ṛgveda there is no specific proof to conclusively prove it.
One of the printed editions considered as a standard publication contains 30 chapters. Only one commentary—the Vidvanmodinī by Yajñasvāmin—is available.
The contents may be briefly summed up as follows: definition of धर्म; limits of आर्यावर्त; sins and sinners; six forms of मर्रिअगे; the four varṇas; ātatāyins or criminals; duties common to all varṇas; the four āśramas and the duties pertaining to them; on Vedic studies; permitted and forbidden ड़ोओद्; rules of अदोप्तिओन्; the king and administration of justice; on पर्तितिओन् of property; प्रतिलोम castes; certain prāyaścittas or expiations; virtues of प्राणायाम and Gāyatrīmantra as puri-fiers; eulogy of Vedic mantras; eulogy of धर्म.
The work refers to several verses of the Ṛgveda. Other dharmaśāstra works like the Mitākṣarā on Yājñavalkya Smṛti by विज्ञानेश्वर (A.
) quote from this work. It has many things in common with the धर्मसूत्रस् of बौधायन and गौतम.

Vāstupuruṣa
(‘personified deity of the site’)
------------------------------------------
Vāstu is the layout of a building site. Before constructing a building there, the land has to be reclaimed from the gods and goblins who might be living there for aeons. This ritual of pacification is known as vāstuśamana. Generally a मण्डल (geometrical drawing), a square divided into 9 x 9 (= 81) or 8 x 8 (= 64) smaller squares is used for this purpose. This is called vāstumaṇḍala.
There is an interesting legend connected with this मण्डल. When शिव fought with the demon Andhaka, a drop of sweat fell from his forehead on the earth. It assumed the form of a fierce demon who attempted to devour the worlds. Then all the gods and spirits rushed towards him, felled him to the ground (face downwards) and pinned him there, all of them being stationed on him. The vāstumaṇḍala contains him with his head in the direction north-east, and, with his hands and legs folded. He is now called वास्तुपुरुष.
If he, as also the gods on him are propitiated, the building will be firm and safe.

vāstuśānti
------------------------------------------
When a new होउसे is built, certain religious rites are performed before entering it. One of them is वास्तुशान्ति or vāstuśamana.
Rice and barley grains are put into a pot of water. A piece of gold is also deposited into it. The owner now goes round the होउसे three times sprinkling this water on the होउसे, repeating the śāntātīya hymn of the Ṛgveda (7.35). It is repeated three more times by pouring the water continuously, chanting three more mantras of the Ṛgveda (10.9.1-3).
This is followed by a होम with आज्य (ghee) using the Ṛgvedic mantras ‘vāstoṣpate......’ (8.17.14).
Preparing ड़ोओद् and honouring the ब्राह्मणस् after feeding them is the last part of the ritual.
Some authorities prescribe that this rite can be repeated every month or in every season or every year.
See also GṚHAPRAVEŚA.

vasordhārā
(‘flow of wealth’)
------------------------------------------
Agnicayana (‘piling the fire’) is an important aspect of सोमयाग, involving quite a few rites. वसोर्धारा is one of them. It is the name of the whole rite in which several hundred offerings of आज्य (ghee) are made with a sruc (spoon of udumbara tree) which too is cast into the consecrated fire at the end. The purpose is to secure all the powers of the deity अग्नि for the sacrificer.
The mantras used are mostly from the Taittirīya and the Vājasaneyī Saṁhitās.
